speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Before we proceed to the question, I rise to what may be described as a point of order. The Redistribution bill was read a second time yesterday, but no motion was made to refer it to a special com-
Redistribution

mittee, but still the order seems to be dropped from the order paper. It should, I think, appear under Government Orders to-day.

As the right hon. gentleman states, the bill was read the second time yesterday, I think, and I understand the government intend to present a motion referring the bill to a select committee. It is in the hands of the government.
It should be on the order paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I may say it was my intention to move to-day for a reference of the bill to a special committee. The reason I did not do so was because I was anxious to make sure, before making the motion, that the number of members on the committee would meet with the general acceptance of the House.
I am not finding fault with the fact that the motion has not been made. I am only pointing out the fact that it is off the order paper. I think it should be there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When the bill "was read the second time yesterday no motion was made for a reference to a select committee and for that reason no motion should appear on the order paper.

I do not agree with that. If the motion had been made for reference to a special committee, and that motion carried, then it would be off the order paper till the special committee reported, but seeing there was no reference at all, it should appear on the order paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Journals show that the bill received its second reading, and I presume it would have been in order to have made a motion to-day referring the bill to a special committee. That was the intention but the fact that no motion is made does not alter the privilege of the government to introduce it. With the permission of the House I would like to say to my hon. friend that the government is of the view
[Mr. MeighenJ
that the work of this committee would be more expeditiously and efficiently carried on if it were a small committee rather than a large one. In 1903 the Redistribution committee consisted of seven members. In 1914 the number was enlarged to nine. The government had thought that if this year the Redistribution committee were made eleven in number, having regard to the different groups in the House, that would be a fairsized committee, and perhaps the most efficient to deal with this particular measure. However, I have gathered that hon. gentlemen opposite feel they would like to have a somewhat larger committee and the government would be quite prepared to concede a committee of fifteen, but I think to go beyond fifteen would make the committee unduly large for the purpose. It does not mean limiting the number to fifteen, because any group may have sitting with their members in the committee just as many of their own party as they may wish to consider the measure. A reference to the rules of the House will show that where a committee is larger in number than fifteen-rule 11, I think, -some special procedure is necessary to have the larger number adopted, if exception is taken to a committee larger than fifteen. I hope under the circumstances that my right hon. friend and members also of the other group will find it possible to agree with the government that fifteen would be a sufficiently large number for the purpose of working out the details of the redistribution. Just as soon as we can get to an agreement on this matter I shall have pleasure in moving the reference of the bill to the special committee.
I did not receive an answer to the question I asked a minute ago as to whether an opportunity would be given to this House to discuss the principles of this measure before it goes to committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yesterday my hon. friend had that opportunity, as every member of the House had. The bill was read the second time yesterday, and if he missed that opportunity, he no doubt on the third reading will have a chance to say something.

I know it is out of order, but I would like to say a word in reference to the Prime Minister's remarks. A committee of more than fifteen does seem large, but the conditions are unique at this time. Of course it presents no difficulty to the Prime Minister on his side of the House, because they will insist upon having a major-

Questions
ity in the committee. That leaves us in a minority of the minority, but our duties are just as onerous as those of hon. gentlemen opposite in relation to redistribution. We had, and undoubtedly will have again, a candidate in every one of the 245 constituencies in the nine provinces, to be looked after. Hon. gentlemen to my left are in the same position. Consequently our work is just as irksome as that of hon. gentlemen opposite. A committee of fifteen leaves us only three. Three were found too few when it was tried. Four were found to be few enough. We have agreed to four, and I put it to hon. members opposite that four are none too many-in fact four are insufficient-to undertake the detailed, burdensome work of reviewing the redistribution of nine provinces and 245 seats.

maintopic: PETERBORO INSPECTOR OF WEIGHTS AND MEASURES
speechtext:
1. The following regulations have been approved by the Minister of Finance, under the provisions of Section 4 of the act of 1922 to amend the Special War Revenue Act of 1915, whereby cheques embossed with words indicating that the stamp tax has been paid, may be used by persons, firms or corporations to whom a license is issued:
July 7, 1922.
1. Application for a license (form L 20) shall be forwarded through the collector of the nearest customs and excise port to the Commissioner of Customs and Excise, Ottawa, hereinafter called the commissioner, in an envelope marked "embossed cheques.''

Questions
The representations made in such application shall be verified by the statutory declaration of the applicant.
2.	There shall be forwarded with the application for license a requisition (form E 159) for the number of embossed cheques required by the licensee, together with a certified cheque, by way of deposit, payable to the Receiver General for an amount equivalent to the estimated tax, as per assertions 1 (a) and 1 (c) on application for license plus twenty-five per cent. The commissioner may at any time require a larger deposit.
3.	Cheques will be embossed and issued to a licensee in the manner and subject to the conditions hereinafter defined.
4.	A licensee shall keep an account in which shall be entered, at the time each cheque is drawn, particulars of the cheque, showing the serial number, the date of issue, the amount and the sum due as excise tax thereon. A separate account shall be kept for each bank or branch of a bank on which the licensee draws cheques. On or before the fifth day of each month the licensee shall forward through the Collector of Customs and Excise at the port through which the license was obtained to the commissioner the account or accounts, ns the case may be, for the preceding month, verified by the statutory declaration of the licensee and accompanied by a certified cheque payable to the Receiver General for the total sum of tax shown ns accrued by said account or accounts; and all bank statements of cheques debited to the licensee's account, and all relevant books of account of the licensee shall be open to inspection and audit for the purpose of these regulations by officers of the Department of Customs and Excise, and such audit shall be made by officers of the department nt such times as are deemed necessary.
5.	When a further supply of embossed cheques is required, requisition for same will be made by the licensee on form E 159.
6. Each embossed cheque shall have printed or lithographed on it, in a prominent manner, the name of the licensee, the number of license and the name of the bank on which the cheque is to be drawn; and no person other than the licensee whose name is so printed or lithographed shall draw such cheque, and no bank shall pay an embossed cheque drawn by any person other than the licensee whose name is so printed or lithographed, or on which the license num-her docs not appear.
7.	In the event of a licensee abandoning his license there may be repaid to him the amount of his deposit in excess of the amount payable in respect of the stamp tax on all embossed cheques issued by him less the cost of embossing and transportation of that portion of unused cheques remaining on hand, and the unused cheques must be returned to the commissioner. If a license is cancelled for a violation of any of the provisions of the Special War Revenue Act, and amendments, or of these regulations, or for any other reason, no portion of the deposit will be repaid to the licensee and he shall be liable for any further amount payable by him in respect of stamp tax on embossed cheques which he has issued and he shall return to the commissioner all unissued embossed cheques.
8.	The design to be embossed on cheques shall be in a form to be approved by the Commissioner and shall contain the words "tax paid" and the number of the license.
9.	The commissioner may refuse any application for a license if in his judgment, which shall be final, the number of cheques issued by the applicant is not large enough to justify the granting of a license or for any other reason which appears to the commissioner to warrant refusal.
10.	The blank cheques must be forwarded to the American Bank Note Company, Ottawa, who must be advised by the shipper as to the quantity and description of blank cheques in the consignment, the outer covering of the parcel being also marked to indicate the name and address of the shipper. Packages, the gross weight of which exceed 90 pounds, if shipped from Montreal, 60 pounds if shipped from Toronto, or 40 pounds if shipped ffom Winnipeg, must be forwarded by freight. Under these weights shipment must be made by express. From each of the three places mentioned the parcels are to be forwarded by Canadian government railways or Canadian National Express (as the case may be), charges collect.
Shipments made from points other than the foregoing are to be forwarded by the same lines where practicable, the method of transportation being determined by cost. If the lower rate is provided by freight, shipment must be made accordingliy, and vice versa.

Mr. A. W. NEILL (Comox-Alberni) moved the second reading of bill No. 6 to amend the Immigration Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I need not long detain the House in this matter; while it is an important one, it is not elaborate in its details. When it was read the first time I mentioned briefly the purport of it. The object of this bill is to confirm in this parliament a right that I think none will deny- its absolute right to control and regulate immigration into this country of whatever source or origin. It is not confined to some kind of immigration, it applies to all kinds. The bill provides that no immigrant shall enter Canada without permission of the Minister of Immigration. Who shall gainsay the reasonableness of that, or who shall claim that that is an unfair provision as regards immigrants or as affecting any other nation?
There is ample provision in the bill under the various sections further on to provide for the entrance of those who wish to come for short periods on account of business or health
or pleasure. In fact there is more ample provision in this respect than is customary in such legislation. There is also provision made for the exemption from its operation of all British subjects-at least, all white British subjects.
Similar legislation was passed in New Zealand in September 1920 after a very full debate. The New Zealand parliament is much smaller than ours, but 30 per cent of the members took part in that debate, which would be equivalent to some seventy-five or eighty members discussing it in this House, and would mean a debate with us of some eight or ten days. So it shows the matter was very thoroughly debated in that parliament. And it is worthy of note that at the close the bill was passed without a division, although there were objections taken to it from both sides of the House.
I wish to quote from the speech of the hon. Premier of New Zealand when he was introducing the bill. It will give a good idea of the point of view from which he regarded the measure. He said, among other things:
Now this bill is the result of a deep-seated sentiment on the part of a huge majority of the people of this country that this Dominion shall be what is often called a "white" New Zealand, and that the people who come here should, as far as it is possible for us to provide for it, be of the same way of thinking from the British Empire point of view-I might have said the Imperial poipt of view, but I say from the British Empire point of view-and that they shall be people who will be loyal to the empire, loyal to the crown, and loyal to this country when they become its citizens. There is no injustice intended to the people of any other country who come here; nothing of that sort. We intend to treat them fairly and well, whether they are here now or whether they come in the future. But the point I wish to make- and I want to emphasize it-is that we have a perfect right to safeguard our immigration policy and to be quite sure that the persons who will come and take up their residence here as permanent citizens shall be people of whom we shall be able to approve.
Further on he remarks:
I have mentioned the question of alien immigrants, and honourable members know that at present what is provided to safeguard foreign immigration is the education test. Well, the education test-and members know it as well as I do-has been of very little value indeed, and we are dropping it. The provisions of this bill will take its place, and I feel certain if we can bring it into operatiop-and I have no doubt of that- that they will be found much more effective. We are doing away with the finger-print as being unnecessary. I know it is very much resented by people who are compelled to leave their finger-prints in this country, and under this bill it will no longer be necessary.
And again at a later stage, he said:
Clearly we want to keep the race as pure in this Dominion as it is possible to keep it. I have not the slightest doubt but that that object will be effected by this bill.
The first objection made by the leader of the Opposition in tb*' New Zealand House

Immigration Act
consisted almost entirely of a protest that the bill had not been introduced sooner. That will give you an idea, Mr. Speaker, of how the opposition there regarded the proposed legislation. In the course of the debate another hon. member said:
There is no question that in recent times we have had grave reason to fear that that policy is being menaced because of the large influx of Asiatics during the last twelve months. So far as the general policy of the bill is concerned, I think the House will agree with the Prime Minister that some effective steps must be taken to deal with the menace, which undoubtedly exists.
Further on he quoted Sir Edward Grey in connection with the Chinese in South Africa and added:
The question is, what sort of civilization are you building up? Are you building up a civilization in which all the citizens are capable of the full rights of citizens, or a civilization the elements of which are bound to conflict in their customs, their habits and their policies? If you are doing so, you are building on an unstable foundation.
And so on from various other members of that parliament. Now, that was the general tone of the debate when the matter was introduced. The objections made were, in the main, three in number, with which I will deal briefly. The first was that the measure might prove to be ultra vires, or at least unfair to the Hindus, who were fellow British subjects and technically and biologically of the white race. "The second was that the matter could more properly be dealt with by means of diplomacy, and the third was that it would be putting in the hands of the Minister of Immigration a dangerous power which might under certain conditions be used unfairly and unjustly.
With regard to the first objection that it might be ultra vires, the people of New Zealand did not appear to have much apprehension in that regard. As a matter of fact, the act was passed by the Dominion and approved by the Imperial government and no protest was made by any nation. It is not necessary, therefore, to waste time in a discussion of that point, because time has proved that it was intra vires.
So far as the objection regarding the Hindus is concerned, the Hindu question is a burning one in New Zealand. There are 60,000 Hindus in Fiji, which is a comparatively short distance from New Zealand; large numbers .of them were at that time flocking to New Zealand, and the question was a very burning one in that country. It may be said that this is a question that does not primarily interest this parliament, because the immigration of Hindus into Canada is supposed to have been stopped. But I wish to warn the members, particularly those from British

Columbia, that the conditions have recently changed. A number of years ago the government of the day passed an order in council which prohibited immigration of Hindus into Canada. This order in council provided that all immigration of persons who did not arrive in Canada by continuous journey from the country of origin should be stopped, and one of the main effects of that provision was to stop the very large immigration then coming to Canada from India, because we have no direct steamship service between India and Canada. The matter was the subject of much discussion at that time, some ten or fourteen years ago, as the British Columbia members well know; it had reached an acute stage when it was adequately dealt with by the order in council to which I have referred. But what do we find to-day? We find that recently there has been passed an order in council which to all intents and purposes does away with that earlier order in council. In other words, with some restrictions which can easily be evaded, the continuous journey has been done away with and people will be allowed to come by a non-continuous journey. I submit that, by the very simplest method of evasion, any number of Hindus- and, what is still more dangerous, their wives and minor children-can come into Canada. So it behoves us to study well this Hindu question in its full significance as regards this act.
We find, then, that New Zealand gave a good deal of attention to this phase of the subject, and we find that it was
4.	p.m. dealt with in this way: When the attention of the prime minister, Mr. Massey, was called to it, he said there was no danger of producing conflict or annoyance or friction; that on the occasion of the holding of the Imperial War conference in 1918 a conference at which India among other nations of the British Empire was fully represented, the following resolution was passed-I need quote only a few sentences which contain the gist of the thing:
It is agreed that it is an inherent function of the governments of the several communities of the British commonwealth, including India, that each should enjoy complete control of the composition of its own population by means of restriction on immigration from any of the other communities.
It goes on to elaborate that further, but that is the gist of it. That principle was not only assented to by representatives of India at that conference, but the resolution was actually introduced by the Maharajah of Bikaneer-if you know the gentleman. He was India's representative at that time-and I may say that he is one of the ablest men

Immigration Act
India has'ever produced. He has since been made a peer of the realm on account of the services he has rendered to India. Any resolution, therefore, introduced by him must certainly have had the full consent of the country he represented. That, in large measure, disposes of the argument that the proposed change would lead to friction with the inhabitants of India. Further, Mr. Downie Stewart, dealing with the subject, made this Remark:
It is pretty clear from the past policy adopted by the British government towards the Dominion authorities that if it becomes a question between the Dominion and some foreign country, the British government would prefer to quarrel with them rather than with us.
This is expressed as regards a foreign nation as well as regarding India.
The whole policy of the British government was well expressed as long ago as at the first colonial conference, in 1897, by Mr. Chamberlain. Nothing could be clearer than what he said: "We quite sympathize with the determination of the white inhabitants or these colonies, which are in comparatively close proximity to millions and hundreds of millions of Asiatics, that there shall not be an influx of people alien in civilization, alien in religion, alien in customs, whose influx, moreover, would most seriously interfere with the legitimate rights of the existing labour population. An immigration of that kind must, I quite understand, in the interest of the colonies, be prevented at all hazards, and we shall not offer any opposition to the proposals intended with that object."
Could the English language be much stronger in asserting that the Imperial government had no intention, has no intention and will have no intention of interfering with legislation of this character? Particularly do we realize that such is the case when we remember that this act has been in force two years and no objection has been registered against it, either by the Imperial authorities or by any foreign government who might think that they were affected under its provisions.
We come now to the second objection that was raised in the House of representatives in New Zealand, and that was that this object could be better obtained by means of diplomacy. Now, I shall not quote the remarks of the one member who took that line; to tell the truth, they are not worth quoting. He began by showing that he had not read the bill in question by taking objection to the non-presence in it of certain features which the premier subsequently showed him were there. He went on the familiar lines that we have all heard so often: he said that the -legislation was crude; that it was not polished, that it was not finished; that the better course would be to proceed by way of diplomacy. He also stated that he had interviewed the Chinese consul, who had declared-and he believed it absolutely-that China did not
32i
want its nationals to go into New Zealand. Have we not heard that before? The Chinese consul also said, according to this gentleman, that the Chinese were a proud nation and did not want to be aimed at in any indirect way- the same old familiar thing that we have heard in British Columbia for the last twenty years, from a different source. He advocated the policy of turning the cheek to the smiter; of giving to him who has stolen your coat your cloak also-a doctrine which was never popular even in the days when it was uttered.
I wish just to mention how the hon. Mr. Ngata dealt with the situation from that point of view. He said: .
As to the method, the hon. member for Clutha. suggested diplomacy as the remedy. Well, it is a very-nice suggestion, but in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, ^he time has come for the British dominions to put their cards on the table with regard to this matter, because they have been far too nice, far too diplomatic, im the past.
But diplomacy does put its cards on the table.

We have before us a very fine example now in the result of diplomacy as between Japan and America. Look at the position America has got into in regard to colonization of the Pacific slope by the Japanese. It may end in war at any time. I think it would be the height of diplomacy if the British dominions were to make it known through the Imperial government to the Republic of China that the view of the people of this country is that they do not desire any Chinese to come into it.
Why not make this sentiment known in a statute? That would surely express the view of the representative people of New Zealand and it would be the authoritative voice of the people of this country. Now, what did the hon. gentleman mean by diplomacy? Our representations would have to be made through the Imperial government-that is, through the Secretary of State for the Colonies. If we adopted that roundabout method we would probably get some kind of reply in four or five years. We would have to make representations at the Imperial Conferences, and so on. It is surely far better for the people of New Zealand to say straight out what they want by statute.
I think that deals practically with all that need be said in that regard.
We now come to the third objection that was raised by the labour members in the House, and I may say that the labour party in New Zealand is a particularly strong and virile one and if they saw any opportunity of finding objections to this or any other legislation they will be far from backward in making it known, so that any approval of any act they passed would be sure to have the approval of labour generally. They raised the point that perhaps the Minister of Immigration might use this legislation not for the purpose for which it is intended-to restrict immigration-but, by a false and malicious use of these powers, to flood the country with cheap coloured labour. They also raised the point, although they were not strong on it, that it was not fair to have British subjects

handicapped. I would like to quote what the leader of the Labour party said in that regard. He said:
When it comes to the matter of considering the possible influx into a country like this of a people whose standards of living are necessarily lower than the standards of living of the people here, and when the people who are coming in do not always know the conditions to which they are coming, then it becomes necessary not only that the legislation of New Zealand shall be framed so as to protect the standards of life of the people of New Zealand, and especially the working people, but that it shall be framed also so as to protect the coloured immigrants who might be brought here. . . . Hence any vote that I give in this House- or that the Labour party gives-will be cast for the purpose of preserving our own standards and for the purpose of protecting t*he coloured workers who may be allowed or induced to come here from other countries.
With regard to the point raised that the law might be abused, that the minister might let in cheaper labour, I have just this to quote. The Prime Minister of New Zealand in replying alluded to it and said:

But in no case shall any such exemptions be made for the purpose-
That was the power of the minister to grant exemptions from this act-

-but in no case shall any such exemptions 'be made for the purpose of an influx of cheap coloured labour, or to bring outside labour from any country whatever into New Zealand during periods of industrial conflict.
Now, as I said, the bill was read without division which shows it had the sympathy of the whole House.
I do not think there is a great deal more to be said. The House will recall the debate which took place here last year on another phase, or one phase-for I am dealing with the whole question of immigration-of our immigration, and that was oriental immigration. We will remember, Mr. Speaker, that the House was unanimous that restrictions would have to be put on. Some hon. members thought that the words "total exclusion" should be used but the majority of the House favoured the use of the words "effective restriction" which they assured us meant practically the same. But unless I have interpreted very poorly indeed the temper of the House at that time, that resolution expressed the desire of the House that we should crystallize into legislation any and all gentlemen's agreements.
To-day the country to the south of us is moving in the same direction as New Zealand, and I have in my hand a bill introduced on February 9, into the House of Representatives at Washington in which I find a provision which excludes from the United States- excludes absolutely without any compromising gestures-and prohibits the landing of any immigrant not eligible for citizenship. Now that in the United States means all those of the yellow races. Unfortunately here it would not have that effect because men of the yellow races are eligible in Canada for citizenship, and a very great and grave error it is. In the United States it is not so, but I merely mention this to show that the government there is going ahead of us in this regard. I see, also, that they are issuing certificates of arrival, which means that every immigrant will practically have to be registered. It is the same thing that we advocated here last year, that all aliens should be registered. The certificate of arrival will form such a system of registration in the States. I only wish to point that out to show that the States are fully alive to the importance of this matter and are really ahead of us in this line of legislation.
We had a pledge from the government last year that something in the way of restriction would be introduced, and it was to be made a matter of possible diplomatic arrangement. The Speech from the Throne has come and gone and there has been no suggestion of anything of the kind. However we know this-

Immigration Act
that diplomatic negotiations take a long time and the fullest measure of consideration must be given to that fact. At the same time I do not know any method more calculated to prevent action being taken, or more calculated to stultify progress than to refer anything, no matter what it is, to diplomatic negotiations. It is practically consigning it to the limbo of the unknown. It may take five years, it may take ten years; we may get a decision in five years, we may get justice in ten. But in the meantime-let us pass this bill. The measure is general in character; it does not apply itself to oriental immigration specifically, but by general provisions which will affect each and every national of the world. I have not mentioned the word "Japanese"; that word does not appear in the bill. The whole tenor of the measure is one of general application, it is applicable to every nation under the sun, including our own white race in India.
I particularly want to emphasize that-to emphasize the fact that there is no possible chance of protest or friction or of diplomatic or any other kind of trouble. It was passed in New Zealand, approved of by the Imperial government, and no protest has been heard from any nation whatever regarding its conditions.
You remember during the war how we all read with interest Bairnsfather's sketches of soldiers at the front, and how one soldier said to his comrade "Bill, if you know a better hole, then lead me to it." If we know a better system of achieving this result by all means lead us to it; but if we do not, are we not logically driven to accepting this measure? If we have in the far distant future the hope of diplomatic negotiations which will achieve the same end by all means go on negotiating, but in the meantime-let us pass this bill.
I would like to make one more quotation from the proceedings of the New Zealand legislature. Two years after the act was passed a member asked the Minister of Internal Affairs how the act had worked and this is his reply:
My own opinion is that the act would be copied all over the British Empire because it was the most ingenious method of regulating immigration yet devised.
The return laid on the Table showed that the working of the act was very satisfactory. After eighteen months of operation that was the considered opinion of the minister in charge of its working. It evidently worked well there and will work well here. But by all means, let the diplomatic duel go on in the meantime. It may not do any good, but in the meantime, let us assist the government by the passage of this bill. I am reminded
here of a legend in connection with a Scotch nobleman. It is more than a legend because there is documentary evidence of it. It happened long ago. It was when the Scotch nobility were fighting in France, but not during the late war. I would like to remind my hon. friends from Quebec that long before there was any talk of friendship between the English and French, the Scotch and ;the French had the strongest rapprochement. Six or seven hundred years ago there was intense friendship between the Scotch and French and great intercourse. When the Scotch were fighting for freedom against the tyranny of the English kings, when the English kings * were holding lands in France, and styling themselves as kings of England and France, the Scotch and French were in great sympathy. The Scotch cadets used * to go to France for their culture and their education and marriages between the Scotch nobility and the French aristocracy were quite compion. Finally Scotland achieved her liberty from the English domination by the simple and characteristically Scotch method of going on fighting long after everybody had admitted that she was beaten. When they were relieved of that form of activity, the young Scotch cadets, who had been trained to do nothing but fight, passed in many instances to France and joined up with the French army. A large contingent of Scotch continued to fight under the banner of the French, and often could be seen the Scottish banner of the Lion waving on the same battlefield as the golden Lilies of France. I explained that because this Scotch nobleman was the leader of the Scotch brigade at one time, and they had been engaged in fighting. There was some sort of war always going on on the Continent, and on this occasion, the French and Scotch suffered a severe defeat, and it was afterwards discovered that it was due to the treachery of a Count Somebody, whose name I have forgotten. He was a count, a man of influence and standing in the country in which the war was going on, supposedly neutral, and the French and Scotch leaders held a conference that night to discuss the situation and decide what should be done. The Scotch leader was there, but it was noticed that he sat apart from the rest. He wrapped his military cloak about him and seemed to be keeping aloof. It was known that he had lost his brother in the battle of the day and it was thought he was nursing his wrath or his grief, and the other members left him alone. This diplomatic conference went on all night discussing what should be done with this count. Some said, "Burn him in his castle and all that it contains." Others
Immigration Act

said, "Court-martial him," and the diplomatic men said, "It is going to cause trouble and incite the ill-will of this' nation in whose domains we are. Perhaps it would be better diplomatically to ignore the situation and merely ignore the man as a traitor, and go on the best way we can." The diplomatic battle waged backwards and forwards. They could not come to any agreement. The night was far gone and it was necessaiy at last to consult the Scotch leader, whose words were as wise in counsel as his arm was strong in battle. They roused him up and asked his opinion, and he came to the head of the table and made his statement. I will have to translate it into English for the benefit of those benighted Sassenachs who never learned the beautiful Scotch language, the language as used in the Garden of Eden. His words were to this effect: "Gentlemen, I have heard your arguments pro and con. Before I came to this conference I was somewhat suspicious, a little dubious in fact, as to the result of the diplomatic conference, and just in case of a miscarriage of that diplomatic justice which you are seeking and to make the thing certain,"-and he unfolded his cloak-"I have brought the head of the Count with me." He disclosed the bloody head of the count whose fate they had been discussing all night. That is the difference between action and diplomacy. A man of action can always put it over the man of diplomacy. Let us proceed along these lines.
I would not be quite as exacting as my Scotch forebear. Let us continue with the diplomatic discussion, with all its legal quibbles and diplomatic sophistries, but-let us pass the bill. I can imagine the leader of the government would go with more confidence into a diplomatic conference if he knew he had this bill passed beforehand. I suppose it' does not make much difference whether you are sitting into a diplomatic game of poker with another nation, or playing with Mr. Jiggs in Dinty Moore's back parlour, if you have the knowledge that you have a fifth ace up your sleeve, it is calculated to give you a better feeling. Let us cut the Gordian knot of the diplomatic difficulty by passing this bill, but if need be, if it will please the nations of the earth, go on with these diplomatic negotiations, you will get a decision some day, but in the meantime-this bill will serve the purpose. We have nothing to lose by it, we have everything to gain, and the risk is practically nil. I would submit to the consideration of the House that nothing can be lost by the passage of this bill to-day.

I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I did not know the hon. gentleman was going to ask for the second reading of this- bill today. There are two things in connection with this bill that I would like to draw to the attention of the House. As far as the bill itself is concerned, I have no particular objection to it. The bill briefly provides that the Minister of Immigration shall absolutely control every person entering Canada and every person must have a permit, unless he be a British subject. I would not take exception to the bill, except that it cancels the present Immigration Act. There are a great many duties which the Immigration department performs for the government, and there are a great many provisions in the present Immigration Act that it is absolutely necessary should be embodied in the bill. Whether or not you should put it absolutely within the power of the minister to say, outside of British subjects who shall and who shall not enter Canada, I am not prepared to say to-day.
I propose to bring down next week a bill that will deal with Chinese immigration, and I propose to embody in that bill a provision for registration. There is no registration here. I propose to embody in the bill a provision for taking the finger prints of those who are leaving the country who desire to return again, because the hon. member for Comox-Al-berni (Mr. Neill) will, I think, agree with me that that is one of the greatest difficulties we have to contend with, in connection with the oriental people particularly. I am not just sure, after having read the bill carefully, whether registration is provided for or not. But those are some of the objections to be taken to the bill. I have no objection to my hon. friend having a discussion of this subject when the government bill is introduced, and when our amendment to the present Immigration Act is brought down and we can then get the consensus of opinion of the House as to what we should have to enable us to carry out the Immigration Act successfully.
I may say that there is rightly or wrongly, prevalent in the Scandinavian countries from which we desire to get immigration, and on the Continent, a feeling based on our present Immigration Act, that we do not want people to come to Canada, owing to the restrictions that we have placed on them at the present time. I do not think that feeling should exist. I think people whom we are desirous of having come to Canada, whom wo are going to spend money on to encourage them to come to Canada-and I speak of the desirable class-should have it in mind

Immigration Act
that the}' will be welcomed to Canada, rather than that provisions are to be set up to prevent their entering this country freely. On the other hand, we need provisions to guard against settlers coming to Canada whom we do not want to assimilate into our national life.
Let me deal, for a moment, with the very question the status of which my hon. friend is desirous of improving, that of Asiatic immigration. It puts the Minister of Immigration in rather a difficult position if, as my hon. friend hopes, and I assume he hopes, the minister must refuse absolutely to .allow an Asiatic to come into this country. I do not entirely agree with him,-indeed, I think, perhaps, that is a mild way of putting the matter-that we would not get into difficulties. Anyone who has been reading the press of recent date, will realize that we have some difficulty at the moment with India with respect to this matter, and it is a very trivial matter over which we are having the difficulty, namely, that of the right of Indians to be enfranchised throughout the whole of Canada. We are trying to handle that in a way to avoid friction, and my hon. friends will agree that there appears to be enough friction in the Near East without our adding to it at the moment. I am not any fonder of creating diplomatic difficulties than is my hon. friend; but we cannot at all times ignore them, and at the same time, I am trying, to keep in mind the peculiar situation that exists on the western coast of Canada. I hope the bill, at least as regards Chinese immigration, will meet the approval of say hon. friend, and we are putting some very drastic regulations in that bill. But to say that the whole responsibility devolves upon the minister; that he must assume responsibility absolutely, whether or not he shall allow an oriental or an Asiatic to enter Canada and, if he does, that he is to bear that responsibility without being backed with some legislation-that is a fairly heavy burden for a minister of any government to assume. At the same time, I think there are many admirable suggestions in my hon. friend's bill, and I am quite prepared to discuss it on its merits with my hon. friend; but I would ask, until such time as I bring down the amendments to the Immigration Act and the Chinese Immigration Act, that action on this particular bill be delayed.
