speechtext: Might I be permitted to make just one more observation, that as regards this bill and the present act, with the single exception of the provision for countries with which we have treaties, the minister has power, under the existing act, to prohibit anybody from coming to Canada.

It seems to me that that ground is rather an unusual one for a minister of the Crown to take, particularly as regards matters coming under his jurisdiction. Apparently, in New Zealand, a minister is quite prepared to assume that responsibility. The people in British Columbia feel that this government has not assumed enough responsibility in reference to this subject. Since this matter was discussed in this House on a resolution which I had the honour to submit, pressure for the exclusion of oriental immigration has been unabated on the part of the public of British Columbia, and we have heard expressions from sources which previously had been silent as to exclusion.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that when my resolution was before the House, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that the government of British Columbia had not asked for exclusion, but instead, had expressed satisfaction with effective restriction. Since that discussion took place in this House, there has been a session of the provincial legislature of British Columbia, and I may tell hon. gentlemen that the result of that discussion was that a resolution was passed unanimously in the British Columbia legislature calling for, not effective restriction, but absolute exclusion. I have no doubt that resolution has been forwarded to the Prime Minister of this government. The people of British Columbia want exclusion; they have reason to ask for exclusion, because conditions are becoming worse and worse all the time, and they are demanding that this government assume some responsibility.
I have been asked by different organizations, more particularly by some of the
Immigration Act

women's institutes, to ascertain from the Minister of Immigration what his policy is going to be and what this effective restriction means, and I have forwarded to the Minister of Immigration some of those communications. A good deal of delay in his replying occurred that, I suppose, being due to the fact that he was necessarily absent from Ottawa a good deal, making his tours over Canada, for which tours I must commend him. When I received his reply, it was to the effect that the government was going to do something this session. He did not say what that would be; but he pointed out conditions as they prevailed at the present time, namely, conditions due to orders in council and legislation which had been passed by the previous government, and let the matter go at that.
What we are demanding is that the government assume some responsibility. In the city of Vancouver at the present time, there are some 2,000 oriental merchants; that is to say, oriental trades licenses have been issued and [DOT] are outstanding at the present time to the number of over 2,000, an increase of 500 per cent in the last four years. That is a pretty serious situation.
I said that some new sources had been heard from, and I would say that the church has come into the discussion. The Lord Bishop of New Westminster, in a public statement which he made not long ago and which is recorded in the press, came out strongly in favour of a policy of exclusion. I have here a copy of the Vancouver Province of February 9, 1923. I read the following headlines:
Would keep the province white, Christian and British Menace of Oriental immigration voiced by Bishop de Pencier
Tells Anglican Synod difficult to keep some parishes going
This article says in part:
Warning against admitting further oriental immigration and the declaration that in some sections of British Columbia control of districts has passed into the hands of Japanese and Chinese, were features of the address of Rt. Rev. A. U. de Pencier, bishop of the diocese, in addressing the thirty-eighth annual session of the synod of New Westminster, Thursday.
"The estimated number of Chinese in British Columbia is about 30,000, as against 16,867 Japanese," said his lordship. "There are comparatively few Chinese women in Canada, while on the other hand 5,654 of the Japanese are females. Seven hundred and forty Japanese children were born in Canada last year. The Japanese own 5.637 acres of land in British Columbia, and 3,614 acres of leased land is in their possession. While the fishing industry is practically controlled by the Japanese, the market gardening is almost wholly in the hands of the Chinese. Chinese merchants are admitted without a head tax into Canada, and in 1921, 1,145 came in under that classification.

Situation at Ashcroft
"The way in which this problem affects us, from a church point of view, is serious. The town of Ashcroft, for example, is now more than half Chinese. The principal hotel is owned by a Chinaman, who, when I was there during my visit last year to the diocese of Cariboo, employed a returned soldier and his wife to do his work. The English-speaking population is so weak in number that it is difficult to keep some of these parishes in existence. The old-settled district of Maple Ridge, for example, has 5,000 Orientals resident in the municipality, and 4,000 acres of the best arable land is cultivated by them.
"Let us earnestly consider this question without the raising of racial feeling and endeavour to accomplish two things:
1. To see that we do not admit into our homes or our homeland undesirable aliens.
"2. Secondly, which is perhaps a more difficult problem, to see to it that this feeling, which would properly cherish and conserve our own right and citi-enship, does not hinder us from putting forth all that energy and zeal, which we ought to exercise, so that we may Christianize those who are strangers within our gates, and who, returning, as they do, to their own land, will carry the Gospel message to their fellow countrymen.
"This is one of the greatest problems with which we have to deal in this province and diocese. Let me once again reiterate what I have frequently expressed in public, that in my opinion it is not essential that we should have our vacant spaces and our material resources settled and developed in ten or twenty, or even fifty years.
' We do desire growth, and we welcome an increased population of the right kind, but it is essential that when these vacant spaces are settled and our natural resources developed, that we should have a province that will be white; that will be British, and that will be Christian.
It seems to me that this government should take some responsibility in this matter. I do not think they go far enough by merely making a treaty with the Chinese, particularly if that treaty is not to go any further than was suggested by a representative of the Chinese government in Vancouver the other day. I have here the report of a statement made in Vancouver recently by Dr. Chilien Tsur, Chinese Consul General at Ottawa, who arrived in Vancouver-this is dated January 31st, 1923- from Peking where he had been conferring with his government.
"The immigration treaty," explained Dr. Tsur, "will provide that China shall not allow labourers to come to Canada. The dominion, on the other hand, will remove the head tax of $500, which Chinese people consider to be a disgrace. Canada wishes to limit the importation of labour from China and both countries seek the protection of their subjects in the territories of the other. These things will be provided for in the new treaty which will shortly be entered upon.
What will be the result of that treaty in regard to Chinese immigration? And what shall we get out of it? As I understand, it is provided at the present time by order in council that Chinese labourers shall not be admitted to this country. So that this will not do us any good. Chinese labourers, like

Immigration Act
others, are kept out by order in council, and all that we shall accomplish, so far as I can see, will be to lose the $500 head tax. The minister may think that we shall derive some benefit from the treaty, but I cannot see it that way. As regards the Japanese, I understand that the government is not going to bring down any legislation at all, so that we can expect the Japanese to keep on coming in the same old way. In default of the government bringing down some effective legislation I submit that it is quite proper for this House to support the bill which has been brought down by my old friend from Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). With him, and with other members from British Columbia, I feel that exclusion is the real solution for this difficult problem. Nothing short of that will do. But if, carrying out the promise made to us by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) last year, the government will give us exclusion under some other name, then of course, as to this phase of the oriental question, we shall be perfectly satisfied. We are not bound by any name; all we want is to have the orientals kept out of this country. I am in favour of the bill and I am prepared to support it provided it is passed on some understanding, such as apparently existed in the case of New Zealand, that if it becomes law it will be so administered as effectually to keep out of the country all oriental immigration.
Now, personally, I do not see why we should not try to achieve our purpose in a straightforward manner, why. we should not have exclusion and call it by that name. But if that is objectionable, and if the arguments which the Prime Minister presented last year are sound, all right, we are prepared to accept a bill like this, provided the government can satisfy us that the effect of placing this bill on the statute books will be the total exclusion of oriental immigrants, just as in New Zealand, for that is the way similar legislation has worked out there. Their law means exclusion, but they call it something else. If we can attain the same end by the proper administration of the provisions of this bill when enacted into law, we will be satisfied.
I do not see why the Minister of Immigration should look upon this as a very difficult matter, because he has behind him a resolution of this House stating in so many words that oriental immigration and the rapid multiplication of orientals in this country constitute a menace to the future of Canada. That simply means that orientals are not desirable people to be admitted. Furthermore, he is recommended by that resolution to see that effective measures of restriction are enforced
to keep these people out. I have every respect for the minister, but I do not think he is alive to the seriousness of this question and to the necessity for taking immediate action, and, above all things, for his assuming responsibility.
We are asking in British Columbia that this government do things. I have letters in my file here from many prominent citizens of British Columbia, men of standing in the community, who say that if effective measures are not put into force to keep these orientals out, in other words, if we do not get the help of the law, then the people are going to take matters into their own hands. Well, we had trouble of that kind some years ago. The Prime Minister knows what happened in the city of Vancouver, because he had to go out there afterwards and settle claims for damages. He is very well acquainted with all the circumstances, which were shortly these:	That
the people then decided to take matters into their own hands in order to bring the government to a proper realization of the gravity of the situation.
May I ask the hon. member a question? Do I understand that there are threats of Bolshevism from the Tory ranks, Mr. Speaker?

I did not say anything about Bolshevism nor about the Tory ranks. This is not a political question in British Columbia. Shortly before I left for Ottawa I had the privilege' of attending a meeting called by the Retail Merchants' Association of New Westminster, which was addressed by no less a person than the Attorney General of British Columbia. He does not pretend to be a Tory, and in fact I think he is not supposed to be one. The Hon. Mr. Manson is held out in the Liberal press of the province as the champion of oriental exclusion. He did not mince matters at all in his address. He said: Something has to be done. We have to make those people down in Ottawa realize where they are at. The Liberal party in British Columbia is urging the Liberal party here in Ottawa to do something, to take immediate action. I am not saying anything about Grits or Tories nor about Bolshevism. I am simply quoting the purport of letters I have in my file from leading citizens of British Columbia.
The same spirit which manifested itself in 1907 is commencing to reappear now, and it is essential for the government to assume responsibility, and assume it quickly. We cannot be responsible for the consequences if they continue their policy of masterful inac-

Immigration Act
tivity. I do not intend to engage in an extensive argument on this question, but I want to go on record as being in favour of the immediate passage of this bill, provided we have an undertaking from the government for the effective administration of its provisions so as to absolutely exclude any further oriental immigration.

Mr. Speaker, we have in this question a very clear-cut issue: Are we to have total exclusion or partial exclusion? The people of British Columbia, irrespective of party affiliations, are insisting upon total exclusion. Last session when the hon. member for New Westminister (Mr. McQuarrie) introduced a resolution on this question the government in their amendment made a most important change in its wording, substituting for "total exclusion" the phrase "effective restriction." The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) informed the House at that time that this was the diplomatic way of saying total exclusion. But the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) did not regard the change in that light and, strong Liberal supporter as he is, he doubted the assurances of the leader of the government and voted against the amendment. Hon. members will therefore understand why those of us on this side of the House should be perhaps a little skeptical about further assurances on the part of the government and should be doubtful if the government are now going to be any more solicitous to accomplish the purpose sought to be attained last session. Not only did the hon. member for Skeena vote against the government on that occasion, but we find the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Munro) was absent altogether, and consequently we were left in ignorance as to his stand on the question. I had expected to see the hon. member in his seat this afternoon, to seize the opportunity to explain his position last year, or state his determination to stand by the unanimous appeal of the people of British Columbia to have total exclusion of Asiatic immigration.
It is not my intention to prolong the discussion on this question. The merits of the matter were fully gone into last year; the injury to the country, economically and socially, was established beyond question, not only by hon. members of the House but by the statements of leading citizens of British Columbia. We know that there is no possibility of assimilating these people into our population; their standards of living are vastly lower than ours. We know that

they have entered into and have become masters of many of the most important industries of the country. Retail and wholesale businesses in the large centres are being gradually controlled by orientals, simply because of the fact that they are able to exist upon a very small margin betweeh what it costs to carry on their business and what they expend. White persons who wish to engage in the same business cannot, upon the standard of living, of education and so on that they naturally desire to maintain, compete with the orientals. The question is purely an economic one; it is not a question in which the pride or the dignity of a great nation is involved. It is not a question in connection with which Japan or China may say that an offence has been committed against their national sense of dignity-it is, I say, purely and solely an economic question. In dealing with our oriental diplomats the government will find it necessary to take a firm, perhaps a somewhat stubborn, hold on the question. But I am assured, in discussing the matter with men who are prominent in diplomatic circles, that if a strong and determined stand is taken by the government and they base their action on the economic aspect of the question, there will be no difficulty in arranging matters so that we shall in fact bring about total exclusion.
People in other portions of the Dominion may look on this matter from a different point of view, but I believe their attitude would be more in the nature of apathy or indifference, than an attitude of opposition to the claims of the people of British Columbia. You have heard the views expressed of practically every public organization of importance in the far western country. You have heard the views of men in public life, members of both the provincial and the Dominion legislatures. You are familiar with the views expressed in the British Columbia legislature. You have heard the representations of boards of trade, of retail merchants' associations, of practically every person in British Columbia who is actively connected with its economic or its social life. You have heard the appeal from all these sources, an appeal addressed to the only authority which has the power to regulate and control the matter in this country, for the taking of aggressive and decisive and definite steps to bring about total exclusion.
We are aware of the fact that the development of the West, in our grain export, in our timber business, perhaps in connection with our mines, and so on, will depend in some degree on the development and extension of our trade with China and Japan.

Immigration Act
But I again assure the House that a line of demarcation can be drawn between, on the one hand, the broad aspects of commerce, the export business, our trade with the Orient, and, on the other hand, the question of allowing Mongolians, a lower class of labour; into British Columbia. I submit that the government may foster the best interests of the Dominion, may encourage trade and add to the prosperity of this country, and do so consistently with the policy of keeping out a class of people who are undermining the work of the people in certain sections of our country, especially in British Columbia, who are unable to compete with those who have come to the province with the influx of immigration as I have seen it in the last two years. I do hope, therefore-and I say this in no partisan spirit -that the government will look at this matter in a broad way and that the bill which they propose to bring down will embody those features which are necessary to bring about not effective restriction, but total exclusion; because just as sure as you provide one regulation calculated to bring about effective restriction, the wily oriental will devise two other methods of evading it, and we shall have them coming in just as fast as the}' ever did.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member representing Vancouver (Mr. Ladner) has made special reference to the economic side of this question. Now, I do not
5 p.m. rise to advocate the unrestricted admission of orientals to this country. But I do wish to point out to hon. members that in considering this question we should keep in mind the last observations of my hon. friend, in which he made reference to the trade aspect of it. No later than last week in this House we had before us demands, particularly from our friends in British Columbia, for increased facilities for storage of grain and for development in the harbour at Vancouver. The immense development and the possibilities of greater development of trade between Canada, China and Japan, were emphasized. Recently it was brought to my attention that the government of India has had under consideration a revision of the trade policy of that country. At the last session of their parliament a committee was appointed to consider the matter of preferential trade within the Empire, and there were presented to parliament tw.o reports, a majority report and a minority report. I wish to read just an extract from the minority report so that hon. members may draw their own conclusions as to how the solution of this
problem affects Canada and how the government should be guided in considering the matter-because whether we wish it or not, these problems are interlocked with the trade possibilities of the country. Both reports agreed upon a policy of preferential trade with the Mother Country, and it was pointed out that that preferential trade might be extended to the other British dominions. But the minority report put in this saving clause:
That the condition precedent to any agreement with the British dominions in trade matters on the basis of reciprocity should be the recognition of the right of the Indian people to a status of complete equality and the repeal of all anti-Asiatic laws so far as they apply to the people of India.
Now, Sir, if there is one province in Canada more than another that has much to gain in trade matters by friendly relations with Asia it is British Columbia and the provinces adjacent thereto.
May I ask a question? Does the minister suggest that exclusion would necessarily involve us in hostile relations with the Orient?

Well, I said at first that I was not discussing the question of exclusion or restriction. I was pointing out to the House the importance of giving very careful consideration to these questions. Let it not be forgotten that acts passed by the parliament of Canada, or debates that take place here, will be brought to the attention of the parliaments in the countries where we desire to do business. It is frequently pointed out to the government of Canada-it was pointed out to the preceding administration and it has been pointed out to the present government-that we should devote more attention to developing trade in Asia. There we find customers that are worth considering, customers to the number of 700 millions. Taking that trade in the aggregate it is considerable; our trade with India, with China and Japan is growing and growing steadily.

Does the minister not
realize the fact that the oriental is a good business man and that he will buy our goods only if he gets them at the right price, not otherwise. It is not a matter of sentiment with him at all but a matter of business.

Yes, the oriental is a good
business man. The oriental desires to do business with Canada but he desires, as do other customers, to do business on a fair basis and to be treated fairly. All that he asks is to be treated fairly, and I think I can convince the hon. gentleman that his custom is worth considering.

I would ask the minister whether or not he has seen a newspaper despatch reporting the statement by the Right Hon. S. Sastri, upon his return to Bombay, India, that he found that his ideas in regard to the enfranchisement of East Indians before he made his tour of Canada had not been correct. He states that there was no prejudice against East Indians at all, that it was an economic matter; and more than that, there was a desire on the part of the people of Canada not to discriminate against the Japanese and Chinese in favour of the East Indians.

I had the pleasure, in Bombay, of lunching with a member of parliament who is a friend of Mr. Sastri, and I gathered from him that Mr. Sastri, on his part, was going to do everything possible to bring about friendly relations between India and Canada, and he expected us to do a little here to help him along.
Mr. JOHN A. MacKELVIE (Yale):	I
would rather imagine the later remarks of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) have the effect of interjecting into this discussion a subject which is not exactly germane to the resolution now before the House. The latter question can, and no doubt will, be considered at another time. I may say, however, that having lived for over thirty years in British Columbia, and having seen this problem, this menace, of oriental intrusion

Immigration Act
grow from small beginnings until it has now assumed proportions that cause it to overshadow practically every other problem we have to face in that province, I have always, in the .innumerable discussions in which I have taken part during that time regarding this subject, endeavoured to approach it with a mind charged with more than local issues, endeavoured to view it with a full sense of the responsibility entailed by those who advocate complete exclusion having regard to international and imperial associations. That aspect, dealing with the constitutional phase of the question, was very ably and fully discussed last year in this House by the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). His arguments left nothing to be said on the subject, and I do not propose to rehash them now.
In reply to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if he apprehends that any difficulty regarding trade relations may arise from the enforcement of resolutions such as this, I wish to warn him that a much more serious difficulty, a much more inflamed state of feeling in the Orient, may very reasonably be expected to arise if this almost intolerable condition under which we are now suffering in British Columbia is allowed to continue, and that serious results are inevitably bound to follow. There will be disturbances which will have the effect of creating far more inflamed feeling in the Orient towards this country than anything that could possibly result on account of restrictive measures which we may adopt.
I gave my opinion to the House regarding this matter last year, and I suppose that those of us from my province will be compelled again to debate this question when the policy of the minister is brought up. I may say I will support this motion, not because I believe it is absolutely the best way of approaching the subject, but because I am always in favour of moving in any direction which will give us relief in British Columbia -and indeed, in other parts of Canada, for the menace is rapidly spreading-from this condition of affairs which strikes so vitally at the very fundamentals of our prosperity in that section of the country.
As far as the constitutional phase of the question is concerned, I am prepared to reiterate what I said last year. If there be treaties standing in the way, denounce them. If there be anything that can be done by this parliament to absolutely put up the bars against oriental immigration of all kinds, let it be done immediately. Before I came to Ottawa I attended a meeting of the provincial association of the British Columbia farmers. A multiplicity of subjects was discussed and various resolutions advanced. Some of them were the subject of controversy, and debated at great length, but one question arose upon which they were united, upon which they did not even take the trouble of forcing the question to a debate of any kind; that was that the United Farmers of British Columbia, along with all other classes in that country, are absolutely determined to continue their fight as long as they can, until we get absolute and complete restriction of oriental immigration into that province.
I notice the minister said something about a proposal which he would advance to this House, looking to more effective restriction of Chinese immigration. So far, so good. We refrain from saying anything upon what is, perhaps, a more serious phase of the question; that is immigration from Japan. But dealing with each and every phase of it, I am convinced that there is only one solution. I am convinced that nothing would satisfy British Columbia, and I am convinced that the time is very rapidly approaching when nothing will satisfy Alberta and other sections of this country than that the government shall stand four-square to the world and say that we exercise the rights which are undoubtedly ours and refuse to admit to Canada any more of this class of people.

The subject of immigration is one of the most important that could engage the attention of parliament. The task of the present administration, in regard to the future of this country, with its financial situation and other conditions, calls for the increasing of its population at as early a date as possible and by the wisest method by which it can be brought about. I am sure the country is looking with interest to see what steps parliament will take in regard to this problem. My hon. friend (Mr. Neill) who introduced this measure has suggested what purports to be a complete policy with reference to the whole subject of immigration and in the consideration of this problem we have gone away from what might be called the national view upon this question to discuss the purely local situation as it appeals to the province of British Columbia. I apprehend, looking at the legislation now proposed, if I followed my hon. friend correctly, that he has taken a measure which was introduced into the parliament of New Zealand and has attempted to adapt it to Canada and Canadian conditions. I am sure that while this discussion so far relating to this narrow part of the
Immigration Act

subject is very interesting, it cannot be expected, and I am sure my hon. friend who introduced this measure will hardly expect, that this parliament will proceed to adopt this bill, as he has drawn it, as the full measure of what we propose to do in regard to this question at this time. We would rather look to the government and ministry to submit to parliament a broad scheme dealing with all these questions and showing the country how the government is prepared to solve this most important problem. I quite agree with the minister as to the inaptness of this measure in a very great many respects. Drawn as it has been entirely from the viewpoint of New Zealand, we are faced with this proposition. In the second clause of the bill I find:
No person other than a person of British birth and character shall (except as by this act is specially provided) enter into Canada unless he is in possession of a permit to enter in the form and to the effect provided by regulation under this act.
In other words, we are enacting a prohibition against the man in northern Europe, no matter what country he might come from, or no matter what country we might look to for desirable settlers, and we are telling him that he is in the excluded class, and that by no possibility can anybody be allowed to enter the country, except he be a British subject under the terms of the act.
The hon. gentleman has read section 2. Will he quote the general provision of section 3?

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman as to the provisions of section 3, but section 3 does not remove the injurious effect of what is contained in section 2. The complaint I make in regard to'section 2 is that this parliament would, if this -were adopted, give notice to every man in northern Europe, outside of the British Isles, that he was a prohibited person and could not come into this country unless he had a permit from the minister, and I think the minister was quite right in indicating to the House that the responsibility which was going to be placed upon him by virtue of that measure was one which no minister would care to assume.
It is quite evident, looking at subsection 2, of section 2, that our New Zealand friends, in dealing with this question, were dealing solely with the oriental problem, but there the immigration question is largely one which is entirely controlled by that problem. With the exception of those of British origin, the men from northern Europe, to which countries we 
may look to people our land on account of the similarity of climatic conditions, do not go to New Zealand when they want to emigrate. They have to deal largely with people of British origin, who come from the British Isles and the Asiatics, and this legislation shows on the face of it that that is what they are dealing with, and it is, therefore, very limited legislation, and not such a measure as we should enact and place upon the statute books of this country.
I make that remark because I think this debate should be adjourned and that the attention of parliament should not be focussed upon this question in a deliberate way until the minister has had an opportunity of bringing down the submissions which he proposes to lay before us in regard to this all-important question.
May I turn aside for the moment to say a word as to Asiatics. I had the opportunity of hearing Dr. Sastri, when he was on a visit to Canada last summer. We have been accustomed to hearing eloquent things about the great Empire to which we belong, and about the great achievements in India, and about the fact that a certificate of British citizenship was the same the world over. That is the boast of the British people. When Dr. Sastri came to Canada he said:
There are one thousand of my fellow countrymen in this country, and we do not ask that you should permit any more to come. We arc perfectly content with the provisions which now exist to prevent any more from coming into this country.
But they are British subjects and they claim the right to the franchise. When the Great War tvas on, their brethren in India volunteered to engage in the conflict just the same as the sons of Canada did. They were not conscripted; they were not dragooned into the conflict. They have the fullest right to claim consideration as British subjects, according to Dr. Sastri's appeal, as men who come from any other part of the world. That argument, I say, appeals to me, and it does not run counter to the theory of the restriction of Asiatic immigration. If there are in this country one thousand people who are British subjects, and if, for reasons, the class from which they come say: "We do not want to come in any greater numbers," any difficulty that might arise with reference to that branch of immigration is entirely removed. But the appeal which Dr. Sastri made in Canada last year is one which ought to come with great effect to any man who has any sense of reason and fair play and who is proud of the fact that he is a British subject. I make that statement entirely apart from the question of what

Immigration Act
our attitude should be as regards the class known as Asiatics, either Chinese or Japanese.

Does the hon. member
think it is in the best interests of any country that the population of that country should consist of white races and Asiatics?

If my hon. friend had waited, I was proceeding to say that I was not at the moment discussing the question of the exclusion of Chinese and Japanese. That is an entirely different subject, one upon which I think our friends from British Columbia, having regard to conditions existing in that province, are very largely justified in the views which they have put forward. But I apprehend this, that when this parliament wants to lay down a policy which has to deal with the whole question of immigration that must be done by a measure which is complete in its nature and which will grapple with the subject in a systematic and deliberate way. With all due deference to my hon. friend who has introduced this measure, I submit that this bill is not one which this House should adopt, nor which it should proceed to dispose of, perhaps, I should say, before we have had the wider measure which will deal with the whole subject.
My stand in reference to the position of a man who is a British subject and who comes from India, is one which, I wish the House distinctly to understand, is prompted by a realization of the fact that his position is entirely different from that of a man who is either a Chinaman or a Japanese. I would, therefore, submit to the House that this measure should stand over until the policy of the government in regard to the whole question has been brought down.

Mr. Speaker, the hon member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has taken a stand which, perhaps, is one which will meet with more or less approval on the part of quite a number of hon. members of this House. He objects to this bill, in the first place, because it is a very general bill and, second, because the chief argument advanced up to the moment in support of the bill, has been based upon the peculiar and extraordinary conditions in one province of Canada. In justification for the stand taken by the introducer of the bill and those who have supported it, I have this to say for the government-and I sajr it with all courtesy and kindness, and yet with firmness-that in previous years, but particularly last year, we came before this House with a very serious grievance. We presented our views in a wholly non-political
manner. We asked for bread and we received a stone. We asked for the exclusion of Asiatics from this country. We received an assurance that we would have effective restriction. So far there has been no evidence of any definite policy whatsoever to give effect to that promise, although, as my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuar- * rie) has stated, in the same resolution which was accepted by the government, and, indeed, amended by them and accepted in its amended form, there was a clear statement, an admission by this parliament that there was a definite menace in this type of immigration. I, therefore, do not think that we are called upon to apologize to the House for advancing as the chief arguments in support of the bill the problem facing the Pacific coast province of Canada, namely, the Asiatic immigration problem.
My hon. friend who introduced this bill and, I think, others who come from that province, do not come to this House and say that this is an ideal measure from our standpoint. But we are endeavouring to meet the uninformed view-and I use that word without any desire to give offence

of many members from the other provinces who, by their numerical strength in this House, reduce us to a position of impotency and absolute inability to secure our rights or what we contend to be our rights. Unless we can persuade hon. gentlemen that this is a problem that must be faced, we are subjecting our province to a possible inundation of immigrants from the Asiatic continent that will make British Columbia simply an adjunct of those Asiatic countries.
Let me bring to the attention of the House and particularly of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a statement made by a Japanese statesman the other day, to illustrate the grave nature of this problem. Before I read the statement, it will be recalled that at the Washington conference, the Imperial Japanese government agreed in the conference to certain provisions to which I Bhall not refer; but it was also reported at least in the press', that the Japanese allowed the question of immigration to stand aside. It was felt, during the early stages of the conference, that that would interfere with a settlement, and we were all surprised, and, I think, pleased' that the Japanese government allowed that question to stand aside and joined with Great Britain, France and the United States in a disarmament agreement. There is a good deal more, but that is all I desire to read to illustrate my point. In other words, the Japanese government, while it waived that problem under conditions obtaining at the Washington conference, now comes forward and is demanding the abrogation, or withdrawal, or cancellation, or whatever term you choose to use, of the "gentlemen's agreement." The Prime Minister will recall all the incidents surrounding the "gentlemen's agreement" between Canada and Japan. It has served as a partial bulwark, shall I say, for Canada against an inundation of Japanese, but only a partial bulwark-I was going to use the term "meagre," and I will give the figures in a moment to justify that view. But if the government of the Mikado is going to demand from the United States government at Washington the abrogation of the famous Root treaty itself, it is quite within the realm of possibility that they will next demand the cancellation of their agreement with Canada. We are not satisfied with the terms of that agreement. We in British Columbia are faced with a very serious condition in regard to that agreement. We have not particularly attacked it, but we have been very restive under it and I tell my hon. friends opposite that the possibility of the loss of e^en that meagre safeguard will be viewed with extreme alarm in the province of British Columbia.
Let me justify my remarks by giving a few statistics, and I shall try to be as brief as possible. I might observe that I am not basing my whole argument on the Japanese situation;
I am taking it as distinct from the others, to which I shall refer in a moment. There are 17,690 Japanese in Canada, of whom, in the one province of British Columbia alone, there are 16,869. In other words, there are fewer than a thousand in all the other provinces combined. Surely in view of that fact the government, and hon. members of this House will appreciate the reason for our alarm. But that is not the main significance of these statistics. I would ask hon. members to follow the figures I am about to give. In 1910 there were 5,005 births in British Columbia, of which 
20 were Japanese. That gives a ratio of one Japanese to 249 whites. In 1915, there were 10,516 births in British Columbia, of which 303 were Japanese, or one to 34. In 1920, the total births in the province were 11,523, of which 657 were Japanese ,or a ratio of one to 17. In 1921, the ratio was further reduced, standing now at one Japanese to every 13 whites. From 1910 to 1921, a period of only 11 years, the ratio had changed from one to 249 to one to 13.
Is not that appalling? Is it not a situation that is fraught with very serious possibilities and consequences unless we face the matter frankly? This House must get clear on this point. Whether or not the government face this question now, the day will come sooner or later, and I believe it is not far distant, when it will have to be faced. There is no escape from it. In addition to the Japanese there are over 30,000 Chinese in British Columbia. And knowing a great deal about the Chinese methods of living and the difficulty of making a census, I am of the opinion that you could easily add 5,000 or
10,000	more to that number. At any rate, there are at least 30,000 Chinese in the province; while there are about 1,000 Hindus. That gives you a total of some 50,000 orientals out of a population of about half a million. And, mark you, that in the face of the most bitter opposition on the part of the people of that province during the last twenty-five years.	[DOT]
In all that time there has not been a moment when the people of British Columbia have not stood up to a man against this immigration. A few years ago in this House I brought to the attention of the government the fact that we had passed 144 resolutions and bills which had been disallowed by the federal government in preceding years, and which showed that the people and the governmental authorities of British Columbia were very serious about the matter. Now I come to the House and inform hon. members that in 11 years the Japanese ratio of increase has changed from one to 249 to one to 13.
Let me deal with another phase of the question. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) sounded a note this afternoon which has always been resorted to by those who are opposed to our view on this subject. And when I say opposed, I believe the opposition is based on ignorance of the facts, because I find that in Ontario, where a few years ago one could scarcely get a hearing in regard to the anti-Asiatic views of British Columbia, to-day we have a very strong stand against the oriental invasion which they find gradually working into their cities. I read in a Toronto newspaper the

other day, the Mail and Empire, an editorial in which it was stated that this country must face this question sooner or later. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, for whom I have the highest regard, and who undoubtedly had the very best intentions, advanced to this House his reason why we should hush up this question and say nothing about it. That reason was one of trade. Let me tell this House that if some effective steps are not taken in ihe near future it will not be a question of considering the effect on trade; it will be a question whether British Columbia is going to be merely a colony of the Orient or a province of this Dominion. That is what y<?u will have to consider, for we shall not have very much say in the province.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) -and I have his words-referred to the enfranchisement of Hindus, which really touches the whole question, to a greater or lesser extent, of the enfranchisement of all naturalized citizens of oriental origin, as a trivial question. It is not a trivial question. Enfranchise 50,000 orientals to-morrow and what chance in the world could we have with a solid phalanx of opinion of that kind, moulded, moved and directed by one line of thought and interest?

You would have
another party in the House.

Yes, but just imagine the effect of most of these people living in our cities or adjacent to them. In presenting this matter to the House, and particularly to the government, I am not expressing any partisan view. I am stating the view of the members from British Columbia and of every citizen of that province. I ask that the government face this question now, and face it frankly. We must state to the world, with frankness and firmness, that this country is going to stand for the exclusion of oriental immigration to Canada. We are not asking for the exclusion of business men or bona fide students who are registered in any of our universities, nor are we asking that this shall apply to travellers or tourists. We welcome any increase of that kind. But we do say that we must rigidly enforce an exclusion law against orientals. If I understand the oriental mind, and I think I know something about it-my hon. friend from one of the Montreal constituencies (Mr. Jacobs) who is quite a student of immigration, 'laughs-I happen to have taken two trips through Japan, I have also travelled through China and the Malay States, and I have studied the question from the knowledge gained by that contact with the oriental as well as during thirty years
residence in British Columbia and the Pacific coast states. I call the House to witness this fact that in California, Oregon, Washington, British Columbia-wherever this problem confronts the people, can you show me any one from the governor downwards who holds divergent views as to the absolute necessity of total exclusion of this class of immigration? Not one. Why, in this very despatch by this distinguished Japanese statesman he refers to the fact that all three of these Pacific coast states as well as others are solidly against the immigration of Japanese. Now, I say to the government, I say to parliament-because after all I realize that the government can only be moved by the opinion of parliament- I say to parliament that the time has arrived when we must make a clear-cut statement.
I was proceeding to say when the laugh of my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) interrupted me, that if I understand the oriental mind-and I think I do-I am right in reaching this conclusion: If you talk in plain, simple language the oriental will understand and appreciate your meaning infinitely better than if you indulge in the intricacies and refinements of obscure diplomatic terms. If there is anything he is a master of it is the subtleties of diplomacy-and if there is anything that this government is deficient in it is that very quality.
Give us some instances wherein they are deficient.

I think we are all of us perhaps less adept at that than the oriental. However, I will let that pass. But you will get very much farther ahead in dealing with this problem with Japanese, Chinese or Hindus, if you tell them frankly but firmly that the determined policy of Canada is to exclude this type of immigrant. Once that stand is taken without reserve you will have no difficulty in my estimation in dealing with the problem from their standpoint.
My hon. friend the minister (Mr. Stewart) says he is going to bring do\3ti a bill dealing with the Chinese situation. 1 assure him that I do not wish to embarrass him, but such action will not solve this problem, and I very much fear that anything he may bring down of a qualifying character will only increase the discontent and resentment of all classes of public opinion in the West on this question.
Now let me say a word or two in regard to the matter brought forward by my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald). He referred to the enfranchisement of the Hindus. I admit quite frankly that not only in regard to the Hindu, but in regard to any naturalized subject the franchise seems to come as a

proper, just and natural sequence. But here is what we are faced with in British Columbia. The oriental is numerically so strong as an individual group or class, and the possibilities of a further influx are so grave, that we have but one safeguard against it: that is to deny them the franchise so that they have no voice in framing the public policy of that province. My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) is not in his seat, but if he were I can imagine an immediate interjection from him that that is a violation of British fair play.
May I say that it'is also a violation of the understanding reached at the last Imperial Conference which the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) attended?

In so far as the Hindus are concerned-and I think my hon. friend has somewhat overstated the case-I admit that it appears to be a violation of those British principles of which we are all so justly proud. But I want to tell this House again that if we were to enfranchise naturalized orientals, then in all probability the next step would be the opening of the doors for increased immigration from their native countries. And the pressure is there. Japan is complaining to-day that, including Korea and Formosa, she has not room for her 77,000,000 people. But the point is not, whether we are going to supply a country for the settlement of Japan's surplus population. That is not the question. The question is, to what degree we are justified in opening our doors to any given class of immigrant who is incapable of assimilation. That is the question we must decide. So far as Japan is concerned, there are many areas on the continent of Asia that are not settled yet, and if time permitted I could soon illustrate my statement. But we are not called upon to solve Japan's problem in that regard, and British Columbia absolutely refuses to be the dumping ground for the surplus population of the Orient. And I think we have a right to refuse. We have a right to resent any such suggestion. Moreover, we have a right to plead in this parliament with the eight other provinces of Canada for support in this matter. We base that appeal on the knowledge that wherever other communities have been brought into contact with this problem, even in a small measure compared with our experience, they express the same opinion. If my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) or the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) would in the next two weeks have a clerk seek that information in Kingston, London, HamilfMr. Steven*.]
ton, Toronto, Montreal-in fact in almost any of our eastern cities, he would find all of them urgent with strong arguments, just as strong as any I am putting forward to-day, against further oriental immigration into Canada.
I say to the government as the active and potent power in this House that it is on their responsibility that some course of action must be taken. The reason I am speaking perhaps so strongly to-day is that I apprehend this measure will stand over because my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior has so requested to allow him to introduce a bill, and therefore I hope the government may be impressed with the seriousness of this problem, and that when that bill is introduced it will be with a full knowledge of all the facts in the case as far as we have been able to give them, not only to-day but on the very complete debate a year ago.

If my hon. friend will permit me a question? Wherein does this bill to improve the Immigration Act except in the single clause that provides for the admission of nationals with whom we have treaties? I want the hon. gentleman to understand that I am in entire sympathy with his views, but I have not yet seen that point dealt with and as it is very nearly six o'clock I should like to have his views before we adjourn.

I think I can deal with that in the few minutes at my disposal. I am very glad the minister raised the point because I had made a note of it but overlooked it. It is quite true, as he says, that under the general act power has been conferred upon the minister to do virtually all that is proposed in this act by order in council. But no minister has up to the present time felt that it was incumbent upon him by regulation to take such very drastic steps regarding the restriction or exclusion of any class of immigration as are called for by this bill. But clothed with specific statutory power, the minister has no choice; he must do it.
Not necessarily.
Virtually he must.
